analysis.one_liner: Makes the House ethics watchdog a permanent law with subpoena power over members.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have written the Office of Congressional Ethics into permanent law and given it subpoena power, never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE) is the independent board that investigates possible ethics violations by House members and staff, but it exists only because of a House rule that the House can change or abolish at any time. This bill would make the office a permanent part of federal law, beyond the reach of a simple House vote, and give it the same subpoena power as a standing committee so it could compel documents and testimony. The bill never moved after being referred to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on an independent body to police congressional misconduct. The bill also strengthens the OCE itself, which gains permanent status and subpoena power.

how_it_helps.text: It writes House Resolution 895 (110th Congress), which established the Office of Congressional Ethics, into permanent law, so the office could not be abolished or weakened by a simple change to House rules.
It gives the OCE the same subpoena power as a standing House committee, allowing it to compel documents and testimony during ethics investigations rather than relying on voluntary cooperation.

It adds safeguards for investigated members: subjects of reviews would be informed of their right to counsel, and invoking that right could not be held against them, and the office could not act in ways that deny constitutional rights.

analysis.who_pays: House members and staff who would face an independent investigator with subpoena power they currently can outlast or redirect through the member-controlled Ethics Committee, plus taxpayers funding a permanent office.

drawbacks.text: Giving a non-member body the subpoena power of a standing committee raises separation-of-powers questions, since Congress has historically kept investigative subpoena power in the hands of elected members.

Even with the bill's due-process additions, an independent office empowered to investigate members and publicize findings could be used for politically motivated referrals, a criticism that has surrounded the OCE since its creation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain is accountability: the one body that investigates House misconduct outside the control of the members it investigates would become permanent and able to compel evidence. The main cost is the risk that an unelected board could pursue politically charged investigations against members. On balance, the bill is a genuine but narrow transparency upgrade, and it never received enough support to have those tradeoffs tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration and Rules committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom O'Halleran introduced the CLEAN Act on March 7, 2017, to make the Office of Congressional Ethics permanent law.
The bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Rules on the day of introduction, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point in the 115th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members who prefer that ethics investigations remain governed by House rules they can change, since the Office of Congressional Ethics still rests on a House resolution rather than permanent law with subpoena power.

for.name: Rep. Tom O'Halleran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CLEAN Act and was its sole sponsor; the bill had no cosponsors.

against.name: House Administration Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (Chair: Rep. Gregg Harper, R-MS)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Pete Sessions, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from the fact that a single Democrat sponsored it and Republican-led committees took no action.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their staff
industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to a permanent independent investigator with subpoena power, instead of one created by House rule that the House itself controls. Its death leaves the existing member-controlled arrangement in place.

industries.industry: Lobbyists and outside groups seeking to influence legislation
industries.note: A stronger OCE with subpoena power would broaden scrutiny of lobbying contacts with members, though the office's existing mandate already covers some of this. The bill never advanced, so no change occurred.
